after.worked_solution:
The curvature $κ(x)$ of a plane curve $y=y(x)$ is given by

$$
κ(x)=\frac{|{y}^{″}(x)|}{(1+[{y}^{′}(x)]^{2})^{3/2}}.
$$

First, we calculate ${y}^{′}(x)$ and ${y}^{″}(x):$

$$
{y}^{′}(x)=4x,\,{y}^{″}(x)=4
$$

Substituting these into the formula for the curvature, we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}κ(x) & =\frac{|4|}{{[1+{(4x)}^{2}]}^{3/2}} \\  & =\frac{4}{{(1+16{x}^{2})}^{3/2}}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the curvature at $x=0$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}κ(0) & =\frac{4}{{(1+16(0)^{2})}^{3/2}} \\  & =\frac{4}{{1}^{3/2}} \\  & =4.\end{aligned}
$$

The curvature $κ(x)$ of a plane curve $y=y(x)$ is given by

$$
κ(x)=\frac{|{y}^{″}(x)|}{(1+[{y}^{′}(x)]^{2})^{3/2}}.
$$

First, we calculate ${y}^{′}(x)$ and ${y}^{″}(x):$

$$
{y}^{′}(x)=4x,\,{y}^{″}(x)=4
$$

Substituting these into the formula for the curvature, we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}κ(x) & =\frac{|4|}{{[1+{(4x)}^{2}]}^{3/2}} \\  & =\frac{4}{{(1+16{x}^{2})}^{3/2}}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the curvature at $x=0$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}κ(0) & =\frac{4}{{(1+16(0)^{2})}^{3/2}} \\  & =\frac{4}{{1}^{3/2}} \\  & =4.\end{aligned}
$$

The shell above is obtained by rotating the curve $y=2{x}^{2}$ for $x\in [0,1]$ by $2\pi $ radians about the $x$-axis, as shown above. For each point $(x,y,z)$ on the shell, the charge density (electric charge per unit surface area) of the shell is given by the function 

$$
d(x,y,z)=\frac{x({y}^{2}+{z}^{2})}{\sqrt{16{x}^{2}+1}}.
$$

Current part:

Find the curvature $κ(x)$ of the curve $y=2{x}^{2}$ at $x=0.$

content.worked_solution:
The curvature $κ(x)$ of a plane curve $y=y(x)$ is given by

$$
κ(x)=\frac{|{y}^{″}(x)|}{(1+[{y}^{′}(x)]^{2})^{3/2}}.
$$

First, we calculate ${y}^{′}(x)$ and ${y}^{″}(x):$

$$
{y}^{′}(x)=4x,\,{y}^{″}(x)=4
$$

Substituting these into the formula for the curvature, we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}κ(x) & =\frac{|4|}{{[1+{(4x)}^{2}]}^{3/2}} \\  & =\frac{4}{{(1+16{x}^{2})}^{3/2}}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the curvature at $x=0$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}κ(0) & =\frac{4}{{(1+16(0)^{2})}^{3/2}} \\  & =\frac{4}{{1}^{3/2}} \\  & =4.\end{aligned}
$$

decision.explanation: Rotating about the x-axis gives surface area ∫₀¹2πy√(1+(y')²) dx. With y=2x² and y'=4x, this is 4π∫₀¹x²√(1+16x²) dx, so the blank is x²√(1+16x²).

after.worked_solution:
We can find the surface area generated when a curve is rotated $2\pi $ radians about the $x$-axis using the formula

$$
S=\int 2\pi y\,\text{d}s.
$$

Since we're given a curve in the form $y=f(x),$ we have 

$$
\text{d}s=\sqrt{1+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x})}^{2}}\,\text{d}x.
$$

Therefore, we will use

$$
S=2\pi {\int }_{{x}_{1}}^{{x}_{2}}y\sqrt{1+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x})}^{2}}\,\text{d}x.
$$

We are told that the limits of integration are from ${x}_{1}=0$ to ${x}_{2}=1.$ 

Computing the derivative, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(2{x}^{2})=4x.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}S & =2\pi {\int }_{{x}_{1}}^{{x}_{2}}y\sqrt{1+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x})}^{2}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}(2{x}^{2})\sqrt{1+(4x)^{2}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =4\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}{x}^{2}\sqrt{1+16{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}

We can find the surface area generated when a curve is rotated $2\pi $ radians about the $x$-axis using the formula

$$
S=\int 2\pi y\,\text{d}s.
$$

Since we're given a curve in the form $y=f(x),$ we have 

$$
\text{d}s=\sqrt{1+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x})}^{2}}\,\text{d}x.
$$

Therefore, we will use

$$
S=2\pi {\int }_{{x}_{1}}^{{x}_{2}}y\sqrt{1+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x})}^{2}}\,\text{d}x.
$$

We are told that the limits of integration are from ${x}_{1}=0$ to ${x}_{2}=1.$ 

Computing the derivative, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(2{x}^{2})=4x.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}S & =2\pi {\int }_{{x}_{1}}^{{x}_{2}}y\sqrt{1+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x})}^{2}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}(2{x}^{2})\sqrt{1+(4x)^{2}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =4\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}{x}^{2}\sqrt{1+16{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

content.worked_solution:
We can find the surface area generated when a curve is rotated $2\pi $ radians about the $x$-axis using the formula

$$
S=\int 2\pi y\,\text{d}s.
$$

Since we're given a curve in the form $y=f(x),$ we have 

$$
\text{d}s=\sqrt{1+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x})}^{2}}\,\text{d}x.
$$

Therefore, we will use

$$
S=2\pi {\int }_{{x}_{1}}^{{x}_{2}}y\sqrt{1+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x})}^{2}}\,\text{d}x.
$$

We are told that the limits of integration are from ${x}_{1}=0$ to ${x}_{2}=1.$ 

Computing the derivative, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(2{x}^{2})=4x.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}S & =2\pi {\int }_{{x}_{1}}^{{x}_{2}}y\sqrt{1+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x})}^{2}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}(2{x}^{2})\sqrt{1+(4x)^{2}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =4\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}{x}^{2}\sqrt{1+16{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14083460/assets/56a380b075d10862170ed9c9a45c07dddff3eaef1ea9fb3109a61cc3d27b5ac4.png)

 

A point $(x,y,z)$ on the surface generated by rotating the graph of $y=f(x)$ by $2\pi $ radians about the $x$-axis for $x\in [a,b]$ has the position vector

$$
\begin{aligned}r=⟨x,\,f(x)\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,f(x)\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ⟩,\,x\in [a,b],\,\theta \in [0,2\pi ).\end{aligned}
$$

First, notice that $y=f(x)=2{x}^{2}\ge 0$ for all $x\in [0,1].$

So, the parametrization of our surface of revolution is

$$
r(x,\theta )=⟨x,\,2{x}^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,2{x}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ⟩,\,x\in [0,\,1],\,\theta \in [0,2\pi ).
$$

decision.explanation: The derivatives are r_x=⟨1,4x cos(θ),4x sin(θ)⟩ and r_θ=⟨0,−2x² sin(θ),2x² cos(θ)⟩. Their cross product is ⟨8x³,−2x² cos(θ),−2x² sin(θ)⟩, whose norm is √(64x⁶+4x⁴)=2x²√(1+16x²).

after.worked_solution:
Recall that for a surface with parametrization $r(u,v),$ the fundamental vector product is defined as ${r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′}.$

In part 4, we got the surface

$$
r(x,\theta )=⟨x,\,2{x}^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,2{x}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ⟩,\,x\in [0,1],\,\theta \in [0,2\pi ).
$$

We first compute the tangent vectors to the grid curves:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{x}^{′} & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂x}(x),\,\frac{∂}{∂x}(2{x}^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ),\,\frac{∂}{∂x}(2{x}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )⟩ \\  & =⟨1,\,4x\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,4x\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ⟩ \\ {r}_{\theta }^{′} & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂\theta }(x),\,\frac{∂}{∂\theta }(2{x}^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ),\,\frac{∂}{∂\theta }(2{x}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )⟩ \\  & =⟨0,\,-2{x}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,\,2{x}^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the fundamental vector product is

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{x}^{′}\times {r}_{\theta }^{′} & =|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ 1 & 4x\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  & 4x\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\ 0 & -2{x}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  & 2{x}^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \end{aligned}| \\  & =⟨|\begin{aligned}4x\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  & 4x\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\ -2{x}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  & 2{x}^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \end{aligned}|,\,-|\begin{aligned}1 & 4x\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\ 0 & 2{x}^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \end{aligned}|,\,|\begin{aligned}1 & 4x\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\ 0 & -2{x}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \end{aligned}|⟩ \\  & =⟨8{x}^{3}{cos}^{2}⁡\theta +8{x}^{3}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta ,\,-2{x}^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,-2{x}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ⟩ \\  & =⟨8{x}^{3}({cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta ),\,-2{x}^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,-2{x}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ⟩ \\  & =⟨8{x}^{3},\,-2{x}^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,-2{x}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the corresponding norm is

$$
\begin{aligned}‖{r}_{x}^{′}\times {r}_{\theta }^{′}‖ & =\sqrt{(8{x}^{3})^{2}+(-2{x}^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )^{2}+(-2{x}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{64{x}^{6}+4{x}^{4}{cos}^{2}⁡\theta +4{x}^{4}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta } \\  & =\sqrt{64{x}^{6}+4{x}^{4}({cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta )} \\  & =\sqrt{64{x}^{6}+4{x}^{4}} \\  & =2{x}^{2}\sqrt{16{x}^{2}+1}.\end{aligned}
$$

Recall that for a surface with parametrization $r(u,v),$ the fundamental vector product is defined as ${r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′}.$

In part 4, we got the surface

$$
r(x,\theta )=⟨x,\,2{x}^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,2{x}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ⟩,\,x\in [0,1],\,\theta \in [0,2\pi ).
$$

We first compute the tangent vectors to the grid curves:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{x}^{′} & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂x}(x),\,\frac{∂}{∂x}(2{x}^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ),\,\frac{∂}{∂x}(2{x}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )⟩ \\  & =⟨1,\,4x\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,4x\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ⟩ \\ {r}_{\theta }^{′} & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂\theta }(x),\,\frac{∂}{∂\theta }(2{x}^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ),\,\frac{∂}{∂\theta }(2{x}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )⟩ \\  & =⟨0,\,-2{x}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,\,2{x}^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the fundamental vector product is

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{x}^{′}\times {r}_{\theta }^{′} & =|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ 1 & 4x\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  & 4x\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\ 0 & -2{x}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  & 2{x}^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \end{aligned}| \\  & =⟨|\begin{aligned}4x\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  & 4x\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\ -2{x}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  & 2{x}^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \end{aligned}|,\,-|\begin{aligned}1 & 4x\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\ 0 & 2{x}^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \end{aligned}|,\,|\begin{aligned}1 & 4x\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\ 0 & -2{x}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \end{aligned}|⟩ \\  & =⟨8{x}^{3}{cos}^{2}⁡\theta +8{x}^{3}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta ,\,-2{x}^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,-2{x}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ⟩ \\  & =⟨8{x}^{3}({cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta ),\,-2{x}^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,-2{x}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ⟩ \\  & =⟨8{x}^{3},\,-2{x}^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,-2{x}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the corresponding norm is

$$
\begin{aligned}‖{r}_{x}^{′}\times {r}_{\theta }^{′}‖ & =\sqrt{(8{x}^{3})^{2}+(-2{x}^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )^{2}+(-2{x}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{64{x}^{6}+4{x}^{4}{cos}^{2}⁡\theta +4{x}^{4}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta } \\  & =\sqrt{64{x}^{6}+4{x}^{4}({cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta )} \\  & =\sqrt{64{x}^{6}+4{x}^{4}} \\  & =2{x}^{2}\sqrt{16{x}^{2}+1}.\end{aligned}
$$

content.worked_solution:
Recall that for a surface with parametrization $r(u,v),$ the fundamental vector product is defined as ${r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′}.$

In part 4, we got the surface

$$
r(x,\theta )=⟨x,\,2{x}^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,2{x}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ⟩,\,x\in [0,1],\,\theta \in [0,2\pi ).
$$

We first compute the tangent vectors to the grid curves:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{x}^{′} & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂x}(x),\,\frac{∂}{∂x}(2{x}^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ),\,\frac{∂}{∂x}(2{x}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )⟩ \\  & =⟨1,\,4x\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,4x\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ⟩ \\ {r}_{\theta }^{′} & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂\theta }(x),\,\frac{∂}{∂\theta }(2{x}^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ),\,\frac{∂}{∂\theta }(2{x}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )⟩ \\  & =⟨0,\,-2{x}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,\,2{x}^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the fundamental vector product is

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{x}^{′}\times {r}_{\theta }^{′} & =|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ 1 & 4x\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  & 4x\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\ 0 & -2{x}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  & 2{x}^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \end{aligned}| \\  & =⟨|\begin{aligned}4x\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  & 4x\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\ -2{x}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  & 2{x}^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \end{aligned}|,\,-|\begin{aligned}1 & 4x\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\ 0 & 2{x}^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \end{aligned}|,\,|\begin{aligned}1 & 4x\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\ 0 & -2{x}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \end{aligned}|⟩ \\  & =⟨8{x}^{3}{cos}^{2}⁡\theta +8{x}^{3}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta ,\,-2{x}^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,-2{x}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ⟩ \\  & =⟨8{x}^{3}({cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta ),\,-2{x}^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,-2{x}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ⟩ \\  & =⟨8{x}^{3},\,-2{x}^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,-2{x}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the corresponding norm is

$$
\begin{aligned}‖{r}_{x}^{′}\times {r}_{\theta }^{′}‖ & =\sqrt{(8{x}^{3})^{2}+(-2{x}^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )^{2}+(-2{x}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{64{x}^{6}+4{x}^{4}{cos}^{2}⁡\theta +4{x}^{4}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta } \\  & =\sqrt{64{x}^{6}+4{x}^{4}({cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta )} \\  & =\sqrt{64{x}^{6}+4{x}^{4}} \\  & =2{x}^{2}\sqrt{16{x}^{2}+1}.\end{aligned}
$$

decision.explanation: On the shell, y²+z²=4x⁴, so the density is 4x⁵/√(1+16x²). Multiplying by the surface element 2x²√(1+16x²) dx dθ gives 8x⁷ dx dθ. Thus Q=∫₀²π∫₀¹8x⁷ dx dθ=2π.

after.worked_solution:
For a surface $S$ with parametrization $r(u,v)$ for $(u,v)\in D,$ the surface integral of a scalar function $f$ over $S$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}S={∬}_{D}f(r(u,v))‖{r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′}‖\,\text{d}A.
$$

Previously, we determined that our surface can be parametrized as

$$
r(x,\theta )=⟨x,\,2{x}^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,2{x}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ⟩,\,x\in [0,1],\,\theta \in [0,2\pi ),
$$

and the norm of the fundamental vector product is

$$
‖{r}_{x}^{′}\times {r}_{\theta }^{′}‖=2{x}^{2}\sqrt{16{x}^{2}+1}.
$$

Next, we substitute the coordinate expressions of $r(x,\theta )$ into $d(x,y,z):$

$$
\begin{aligned}d(r(x,\theta )) & =\frac{x({y}^{2}+{z}^{2})}{\sqrt{16{x}^{2}+1}} \\  & =\frac{x((2{x}^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )^{2}+(2{x}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )^{2})}{\sqrt{16{x}^{2}+1}} \\  & =\frac{4{x}^{5}({cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta )}{\sqrt{16{x}^{2}+1}} \\  & =\frac{4{x}^{5}}{\sqrt{16{x}^{2}+1}}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, our surface integral can be written as 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}d(x,y,z)\,\text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}d(r(x,\theta ))‖{r}_{x}^{′}\times {r}_{\theta }^{′}‖\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\,\frac{4{x}^{5}}{\sqrt{16{x}^{2}+1}}\cdot 2{x}^{2}\sqrt{16{x}^{2}+1}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\,8{x}^{7}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}8{x}^{7}\,\text{d}x\cdot {\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =[{x}^{8}]_{0}^{1}\cdot [\theta ]_{0}^{2\pi } \\  & =(1-0)\cdot (2\pi -0) \\  & =2\pi .\end{aligned}

For a surface $S$ with parametrization $r(u,v)$ for $(u,v)\in D,$ the surface integral of a scalar function $f$ over $S$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}S={∬}_{D}f(r(u,v))‖{r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′}‖\,\text{d}A.
$$

Previously, we determined that our surface can be parametrized as

$$
r(x,\theta )=⟨x,\,2{x}^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,2{x}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ⟩,\,x\in [0,1],\,\theta \in [0,2\pi ),
$$

and the norm of the fundamental vector product is

$$
‖{r}_{x}^{′}\times {r}_{\theta }^{′}‖=2{x}^{2}\sqrt{16{x}^{2}+1}.
$$

Next, we substitute the coordinate expressions of $r(x,\theta )$ into $d(x,y,z):$

$$
\begin{aligned}d(r(x,\theta )) & =\frac{x({y}^{2}+{z}^{2})}{\sqrt{16{x}^{2}+1}} \\  & =\frac{x((2{x}^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )^{2}+(2{x}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )^{2})}{\sqrt{16{x}^{2}+1}} \\  & =\frac{4{x}^{5}({cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta )}{\sqrt{16{x}^{2}+1}} \\  & =\frac{4{x}^{5}}{\sqrt{16{x}^{2}+1}}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, our surface integral can be written as 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}d(x,y,z)\,\text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}d(r(x,\theta ))‖{r}_{x}^{′}\times {r}_{\theta }^{′}‖\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\,\frac{4{x}^{5}}{\sqrt{16{x}^{2}+1}}\cdot 2{x}^{2}\sqrt{16{x}^{2}+1}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\,8{x}^{7}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}8{x}^{7}\,\text{d}x\cdot {\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =[{x}^{8}]_{0}^{1}\cdot [\theta ]_{0}^{2\pi } \\  & =(1-0)\cdot (2\pi -0) \\  & =2\pi .\end{aligned}
$$

content.worked_solution:
For a surface $S$ with parametrization $r(u,v)$ for $(u,v)\in D,$ the surface integral of a scalar function $f$ over $S$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}S={∬}_{D}f(r(u,v))‖{r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′}‖\,\text{d}A.
$$

Previously, we determined that our surface can be parametrized as

$$
r(x,\theta )=⟨x,\,2{x}^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,2{x}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ⟩,\,x\in [0,1],\,\theta \in [0,2\pi ),
$$

and the norm of the fundamental vector product is

$$
‖{r}_{x}^{′}\times {r}_{\theta }^{′}‖=2{x}^{2}\sqrt{16{x}^{2}+1}.
$$

Next, we substitute the coordinate expressions of $r(x,\theta )$ into $d(x,y,z):$

$$
\begin{aligned}d(r(x,\theta )) & =\frac{x({y}^{2}+{z}^{2})}{\sqrt{16{x}^{2}+1}} \\  & =\frac{x((2{x}^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )^{2}+(2{x}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )^{2})}{\sqrt{16{x}^{2}+1}} \\  & =\frac{4{x}^{5}({cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta )}{\sqrt{16{x}^{2}+1}} \\  & =\frac{4{x}^{5}}{\sqrt{16{x}^{2}+1}}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, our surface integral can be written as 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}d(x,y,z)\,\text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}d(r(x,\theta ))‖{r}_{x}^{′}\times {r}_{\theta }^{′}‖\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\,\frac{4{x}^{5}}{\sqrt{16{x}^{2}+1}}\cdot 2{x}^{2}\sqrt{16{x}^{2}+1}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\,8{x}^{7}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}8{x}^{7}\,\text{d}x\cdot {\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =[{x}^{8}]_{0}^{1}\cdot [\theta ]_{0}^{2\pi } \\  & =(1-0)\cdot (2\pi -0) \\  & =2\pi .\end{aligned}
$$

decision.explanation: The Jacobian columns are partial derivatives with respect to x and θ. Thus a=∂x/∂θ=0, b=∂(2x²cos(θ))/∂x=4xcos(θ), and c=∂(2x²sin(θ))/∂θ=2x²cos(θ). Their sum is (4x+2x²)cos(θ).

after.worked_solution:
Suppose a transformation $f:{R}^{n}\to {R}^{m}$ is defined by 

$$
f:[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ ⋮ \\ {x}_{n}\end{aligned}]⟶[\begin{aligned}{f}_{1}({x}_{1},{x}_{2},…,{x}_{n}) \\ {f}_{2}({x}_{1},{x}_{2},…,{x}_{n}) \\ ⋮ \\ {f}_{m}({x}_{1},{x}_{2},…,{x}_{n})\end{aligned}],
$$

 

where ${f}_{1},{f}_{2},…,{f}_{m}$ are scalar functions with $n$ variables. If $f$ is differentiable at $x,$ then the total derivative of $f$ at $x,$ denoted ${f}^{′}(x),$ is given by the $m\times n$ matrix

$$
{f}^{′}(x)=[\begin{aligned}\frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂{x}_{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂{x}_{n}} \\ \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂{x}_{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂{x}_{n}} \\ ⋮ & ⋮ & ⋮ & ⋮ \\ \frac{∂{f}_{m}}{∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{∂{f}_{m}}{∂{x}_{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{∂{f}_{m}}{∂{x}_{n}}\end{aligned}].
$$

In our case, we have the following:

$$
{r}^{′}(x)=[\begin{aligned}\frac{∂{r}_{1}}{∂x} & \frac{∂{r}_{1}}{∂\theta } \\ \frac{∂{r}_{2}}{∂x} & \frac{∂{r}_{2}}{∂\theta } \\ \frac{∂{r}_{3}}{∂x} & \frac{∂{r}_{3}}{∂\theta }\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}| & | \\ {r}_{x}^{′} & {r}_{\theta }^{′} \\ | & |\end{aligned}]
$$

We computed the partial derivatives in part 5:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{x}^{′}=[\begin{aligned}\frac{∂}{∂x}(x) \\ \frac{∂}{∂x}(2{x}^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ) \\ \frac{∂}{∂x}(2{x}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 4x\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\ 4x\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \end{aligned}]\,{r}_{\theta }^{′}=[\begin{aligned}\frac{∂}{∂\theta }(x) \\ \frac{∂}{∂\theta }(2{x}^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ) \\ \frac{∂}{∂\theta }(2{x}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ -2{x}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\ 2{x}^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
{r}^{′}(x)=[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 4x\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  & -2{x}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\ 4x\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  & 2{x}^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \end{aligned}].
$$

Thus, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}a+b+c & =0+4x\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +2{x}^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & =(2{x}^{2}+4x)\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}

Suppose a transformation $f:{R}^{n}\to {R}^{m}$ is defined by 

$$
f:[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ ⋮ \\ {x}_{n}\end{aligned}]⟶[\begin{aligned}{f}_{1}({x}_{1},{x}_{2},…,{x}_{n}) \\ {f}_{2}({x}_{1},{x}_{2},…,{x}_{n}) \\ ⋮ \\ {f}_{m}({x}_{1},{x}_{2},…,{x}_{n})\end{aligned}],
$$

 

where ${f}_{1},{f}_{2},…,{f}_{m}$ are scalar functions with $n$ variables. If $f$ is differentiable at $x,$ then the total derivative of $f$ at $x,$ denoted ${f}^{′}(x),$ is given by the $m\times n$ matrix

$$
{f}^{′}(x)=[\begin{aligned}\frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂{x}_{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂{x}_{n}} \\ \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂{x}_{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂{x}_{n}} \\ ⋮ & ⋮ & ⋮ & ⋮ \\ \frac{∂{f}_{m}}{∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{∂{f}_{m}}{∂{x}_{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{∂{f}_{m}}{∂{x}_{n}}\end{aligned}].
$$

In our case, we have the following:

$$
{r}^{′}(x)=[\begin{aligned}\frac{∂{r}_{1}}{∂x} & \frac{∂{r}_{1}}{∂\theta } \\ \frac{∂{r}_{2}}{∂x} & \frac{∂{r}_{2}}{∂\theta } \\ \frac{∂{r}_{3}}{∂x} & \frac{∂{r}_{3}}{∂\theta }\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}| & | \\ {r}_{x}^{′} & {r}_{\theta }^{′} \\ | & |\end{aligned}]
$$

We computed the partial derivatives in part 5:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{x}^{′}=[\begin{aligned}\frac{∂}{∂x}(x) \\ \frac{∂}{∂x}(2{x}^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ) \\ \frac{∂}{∂x}(2{x}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 4x\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\ 4x\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \end{aligned}]\,{r}_{\theta }^{′}=[\begin{aligned}\frac{∂}{∂\theta }(x) \\ \frac{∂}{∂\theta }(2{x}^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ) \\ \frac{∂}{∂\theta }(2{x}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ -2{x}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\ 2{x}^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
{r}^{′}(x)=[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 4x\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  & -2{x}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\ 4x\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  & 2{x}^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \end{aligned}].
$$

Thus, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}a+b+c & =0+4x\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +2{x}^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & =(2{x}^{2}+4x)\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

content.worked_solution:
Suppose a transformation $f:{R}^{n}\to {R}^{m}$ is defined by 

$$
f:[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ ⋮ \\ {x}_{n}\end{aligned}]⟶[\begin{aligned}{f}_{1}({x}_{1},{x}_{2},…,{x}_{n}) \\ {f}_{2}({x}_{1},{x}_{2},…,{x}_{n}) \\ ⋮ \\ {f}_{m}({x}_{1},{x}_{2},…,{x}_{n})\end{aligned}],
$$

 

where ${f}_{1},{f}_{2},…,{f}_{m}$ are scalar functions with $n$ variables. If $f$ is differentiable at $x,$ then the total derivative of $f$ at $x,$ denoted ${f}^{′}(x),$ is given by the $m\times n$ matrix

$$
{f}^{′}(x)=[\begin{aligned}\frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂{x}_{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂{x}_{n}} \\ \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂{x}_{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂{x}_{n}} \\ ⋮ & ⋮ & ⋮ & ⋮ \\ \frac{∂{f}_{m}}{∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{∂{f}_{m}}{∂{x}_{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{∂{f}_{m}}{∂{x}_{n}}\end{aligned}].
$$

In our case, we have the following:

$$
{r}^{′}(x)=[\begin{aligned}\frac{∂{r}_{1}}{∂x} & \frac{∂{r}_{1}}{∂\theta } \\ \frac{∂{r}_{2}}{∂x} & \frac{∂{r}_{2}}{∂\theta } \\ \frac{∂{r}_{3}}{∂x} & \frac{∂{r}_{3}}{∂\theta }\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}| & | \\ {r}_{x}^{′} & {r}_{\theta }^{′} \\ | & |\end{aligned}]
$$

We computed the partial derivatives in part 5:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{x}^{′}=[\begin{aligned}\frac{∂}{∂x}(x) \\ \frac{∂}{∂x}(2{x}^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ) \\ \frac{∂}{∂x}(2{x}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 4x\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\ 4x\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \end{aligned}]\,{r}_{\theta }^{′}=[\begin{aligned}\frac{∂}{∂\theta }(x) \\ \frac{∂}{∂\theta }(2{x}^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ) \\ \frac{∂}{∂\theta }(2{x}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ -2{x}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\ 2{x}^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
{r}^{′}(x)=[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 4x\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  & -2{x}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\ 4x\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  & 2{x}^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \end{aligned}].
$$

Thus, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}a+b+c & =0+4x\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +2{x}^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & =(2{x}^{2}+4x)\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$
